content.title: About
content.content: Canned mackerel is fish caught in open seas, cleaned, cut into fillets and sealed in a metal can with added salt, vegetable oil, or tomato sauce. Mackerel is rich in omega‑3 fatty acids, vitamins D and B12, and minerals such as selenium and iodine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mackerel belongs to the herring family and inhabits temperate and subtropical oceans.
Canning preserves the fish’s nutritional value for up to 3‑5 years without refrigeration.
In Japan, mackerel is often served as “saba” – grilled, but in cans it retains a soft texture.
Canned mackerel is one of the most affordable sources of omega‑3.
In Russia, canned mackerel is traditionally used in salads, sandwiches, and as a standalone snack.

items.title: Rich source of omega‑3
items.content: Omega‑3 fatty acids support heart health, lower triglyceride levels, and have anti‑inflammatory effects.

items.title: High vitamin D content
items.content: Vitamin D aids calcium absorption, supporting bone health and the immune system.

items.title: Vitamin B12 and selenium
items.content: B12 is essential for red blood cell formation, while selenium protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low‑calorie protein source
items.content: Canned mackerel provides about 20 g of protein per 100 g, making it a good choice for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Supports thyroid function
items.content: Iodine present in the fish is necessary for thyroid hormone synthesis.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned products often contain high amounts of salt, which can be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish or seafood.

items.title: Bisphenol A in packaging
items.content: Metal cans may have trace amounts of BPA; choose products from reputable manufacturers.

items.title: Potential contaminants
items.content: Like other marine fish, mackerel can accumulate mercury and other heavy metals; moderate consumption is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mackerel can be eaten straight from the can, added to salads, pasta, rice dishes, or spread on bread. It can be gently warmed, but prolonged heating may reduce omega‑3 levels.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, transfer the fish to an airtight container and consume within 2‑3 days, keeping it refrigerated.
